Take a model that has just politely declined to explain how to assemble something explosive. Without touching a single weight, without retraining, without slipping it a clever prompt — you add a small vector to its internal activations at the tenth layer. And in response to the very same request the model begins eagerly writing out the instructions. You did not crack it with words — you cracked it with its geometry. And then you add another vector — and it suddenly tells only the truth where before it lied. This is activation steering: a rudder inserted straight into the stream of thought, bypassing both training and text.

The classic demonstration, from the Activation Addition (ActAdd) paper by Turner and co-authors, is the "love minus hate vector." You take two short contrasting prompts, "Love" and "Hate," run them through the model, read off the activations at a chosen layer, and subtract one from the other. What you get is a direction in representation space — the "axis of love." Add it with a positive coefficient to the activations during generation on any neutral topic — and the text warms up, becomes about tenderness and closeness. Add it with a negative one — and it cools. By the same recipe one builds an "anger vector," a "weddings vector," a "conspiracy-theories vector." One contrast — one direction — one volume knob.

The mechanism and its significance. Underneath it all is the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that abstract features — tone, truthfulness, topic, the intent to refuse — are encoded in the activations approximately linearly, as directions in a high-dimensional space. If so, then a "trait" can be not only read by linear probing (training a linear model to predict a feature from activations) but also written, by shifting the activation along the requisite axis. Representation engineering (RepE), in the work of Zou and co-authors, turns this into a whole "top-down" program: first isolate the direction responsible for a concept (reading), then use it to steer the model (control). Their flagship demonstration is the "honesty vector": they find a direction along which the model distinguishes a sincere answer from a lie, and, suppressing or amplifying it, make the model either lie more eagerly or blurt out the unvarnished truth. Using the same direction, one can also detect that the model is lying, reading its activations as a lie detector.

On one hand — cheap, pinpoint, reversible control: no fine-tuning needed, no labeling of thousands of examples, no expensive reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF); a couple of contrasting phrases and a single vector addition at inference suffice. On the other — it is a window inward: the very fact that "honesty" or "refusal" lives along a concrete direction is already a claim about how the model is built, checkable and falsifiable. Control and interpretability merge: you understand the model exactly as far as you can steer it, and vice versa.

And the same blade cuts the other way. If a "refusal vector" exists, then it can be not only amplified but also subtracted — the ability to say "no" can be suppressed. Arditi and co-authors showed that refusal in open-weights models is mediated by literally a single direction: remove its projection from the activations (ablation) — and the safety restrictions collapse across a broad class of harmful requests, without a single step of fine-tuning. The jailbreak moves from the realm of words into the realm of linear algebra.

How it came about. Doing arithmetic with internal vectors is nothing new — as far back as word2vec, with its "king minus man plus woman," we got used to the idea that meanings add up. In 2022 ROME and related knowledge-editing methods (model editing) appeared, showing that concrete facts can be written into the weights through a local intervention. A separate line of work comes from Subramani and co-authors, who were extracting "steering vectors" as early as 2022. But in 2023 two research teams, almost simultaneously, shaped the approach into a finished paradigm. Alexander Matt Turner with co-authors (a team that grew out of the alignment-research community) released Activation Addition (ActAdd) — a minimalist, almost bare-bones recipe: contrast, difference, addition. Andy Zou with a large group (including researchers from the Center for AI Safety) rolled out Representation Engineering — an ambitious frame that put activations at the center of AI safety work and treated honesty, emotions, power, morality as readable-and-steerable directions. From there the line of work grew instantly: Panickssery and co-authors formalized Contrastive Activation Addition (averaging differences over many pairs), and in 2024 Anthropic, using sparse autoencoders to decompose activations into features, made the famous Golden Gate Claude — a model with the "Golden Gate Bridge" feature turned up, so that it obsessively steers any conversation to the bridge.

Criticism / arguments against. First and foremost: fragility and side effects. A shift along the "right" axis is almost never clean: representation space is densely packed, the directions are not orthogonal, and, in dialing up "fun," you also break coherence, factual accuracy, or arithmetic. Too weak a coefficient — no effect; too strong — the model collapses into incoherence or loops (that same Golden Gate Claude is, in essence, a caricature of an overdose). Often no coefficient strikes that balance at all, and where one does, the value that works varies from layer to layer and from topic to topic.

Second: the incompleteness of the linear representation hypothesis. Much of what matters to us does not lie along one tidy direction. Some features are nonlinear, distributed, context-dependent; "honesty in general" may turn out to be not a single vector but a family of different mechanisms, glued into one only on average over the dataset. A vector found on one set of contrasts falls apart on another — the generalization is deceptive.

Third, and most insidious: the illusion of control. An elegant demonstration ("look, an honesty vector!") easily gets mistaken for understanding, when in fact it is only a correlation on a narrow distribution. You may have isolated not "truthfulness" but "the style of a confident answer" or an artifact of the prompt format. A model "made honest" by a shift begins, under pressure or on off-distribution input, to weasel again — because you tweaked the indicator rather than removing the cause. This is exactly the trap against which all of interpretability warns: resembling an explanation does not mean being one.

Fourth: misuse. The cheapness and reversibility that make the method convenient for safety make it just as convenient for attack. For open-weights models, an activation jailbreak — removal of the refusal direction — makes any "aligned" model compliant in a matter of minutes, and no safety-tuning of the weights prevents this, because the intervention acts on activations at inference. A defense that lives in a single direction is a defense that can be switched off by a single subtraction.

What to do about it / where it leads. The sober view: activation steering is not a panacea for alignment but a powerful research probe and a pinpoint tool. As a means of reading it is already useful — detectors of deception, of hallucinations, of "the model knows that it doesn't know" are built on the same directions and provide cheap monitoring for any request. As a means of writing it demands discipline: measure the collateral damage (not only "became more honest" but also "what broke"), check generalization outside the training distribution, and do not confuse shifting the indicator with actually correcting the behavior.

Strategically, several lines of work grow out of RepE. Circuit breakers and related approaches (Zou and co-authors, 2024) already use representation control as a built-in defense — not filtering the output but redirecting internal states away from harmful trajectories. Sparse autoencoders promise to replace crude contrastive vectors with a decomposition into interpretable, less entangled features — so as to dial up "honesty" without touching "arithmetic." And the theme of dual use poses an inconvenient but honest question for open-weights policy as a whole: if safety restrictions are linearly removable at inference, then "aligned" open weights cannot be considered protected by construction, and one must rely on layers of defense outside the model.

Above all, though, this line of work shifted the perspective: it turned the internal activations from a murky "black box" into a space in which concepts have addresses and behavior has handles. This is at once the most reassuring and the most alarming upshot: if we have learned to find and pull these handles, so will anyone who wants to pull the other way.
